summary: WISE 0855-0714 is a known brown dwarf, an object too small to burn hydrogen like a star, and the coldest one known. It sits about 7.3 light-years away. WANDERERS saw it shift 131 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026, about 8.27 arcseconds per year, within 1.5% of the catalogue's 8.15. It shines 5.1 times brighter near 4 to 4.75 microns than at 3.3 microns, where methane absorbs light. It is too faint for Gaia's camera. Of 158 spectrum points, 41 are flagged, but all three checks passed, so confidence is high.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Two clues agree. It moved 131 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026, about 8.27 per year, within 1.5% of the published 8.15. That shows we are tracking the right object, and a very nearby one. It is also 5.1 times brighter at 4 to 4.75 microns than in the 3.3 micron methane band, the dip methane causes in cold atmospheres. Gaia cannot see it, and 41 of 158 spectrum points are flagged.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: 41 of the 158 spectrum points are flagged, and the 3.3 µm brightness has an error bar of about 28%, so the 5.1× methane test could move. The spectrum is unusually bright below 1 µm for something this cold, which suggests light from a nearby star is mixed in. The north-south part of the motion also disagrees: 845 measured versus 673 catalogued, in thousandths of an arcsecond per year.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE recorded this patch of sky around 2010, and SPHEREx imaged it again in 2025 and 2026. Over that gap of almost 16 years, WISE 0855-0714 moved 131 arcseconds, about 21 SPHEREx pixels. That works out to 8.27 arcseconds per year, close to the catalogue's 8.15. SPHEREx also splits light into many colors. That shows the methane dip of a cold brown dwarf. However, 41 of 158 spectrum points are flagged.
